StructuralRule.Notes: Contingency rule for 4D8CE40F against Sequelize.query()
StructuralRule.Predicate: FunctionCall fc: possibleTargets contains [Function: name == "query" and ( enclosingClass.supers contains [Class: name == "Sequelize"] or fc.instance.possibleTypes contains [Type: name == "Sequelize"] ) ] and arguments[0] is [Expression arg: arg.constantValue.null]

StructuralRule.Notes: This rule is written to match dataflow XSS rules such as CA4335F, so SCA (22.2) can overwrite it by them. Note: dataflow XSS rules are matches with type NSTNonstaticFieldAccess. See notes on CA4335F for details. Also this rule doesn't overwrite E9DDEB53 after consulting Justin.

/* find a lambda that calls a function that assigns a value to a field */ FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: ( ( name matches "send|bind|createSocket|createServer|get|request|addListener|once|resolve(4|6|Cname|Mx|Ns|Soa|Srv|Txt)?|lookup(Service)?|reverse|exec(File)?" and possibleHeapPaths contains [String str: str matches "dgram(\.Socket)?|http(s)?|net|tls|dns|child_process"] ) or ( name == "on" and not possibleHeapPaths contains [String str2: str2 matches "HTML[A-z]*Element.*|(\$)?window|(\$)?document"] and not fc.instance is [FunctionCall: possibleTargets contains [Function: name matches "jQuery|\$" or (name == "constructor" and possibleHeapPaths contains [String: matches "(jQuery|\$)\.(prototype|fn)"]) /* account for jQuery selector filters */ or name matches "eq|filter|first|has|is|last|map|not|slice|children|closest|find|((next|prev)(All|Until)?)|offsetParent|parent|parents|parentsUntil|siblings|add|addBack|andSelf|end|not|contents|each" ] ] and not fc.instance.possibleHeapPaths contains "angular.element" and fc.arguments.length == 2 ) )] and fc.arguments contains [Expression e: possibleFunctionTargets contains [Function: contains [FunctionCall: function is [Function lambda: /* lambda isn't recursive */ not lambda contains [FunctionCall recursiveFC: recursiveFC == fc or recursiveFC.function contains [FunctionCall: == fc]] and lambda contains [Location loc: loc.type.arrayDimensions == 0 and loc in [AssignmentStatement: lhs.location is [Location l: l.transitiveBase === loc.transitiveBase]] /* isn't ~parent field that seems to be specified around lambdas */ and not loc.sourceLocation.null /* isn't length field in NST */ and loc.name != "length" /* isn't 'this' */ and loc.name != "this" and not loc.name startsWith "~" and fc.enclosingFunction contains [Location loc2: loc2.type.arrayDimensions == 0 and loc2.name == loc.name /* the underlying declaration is the same i.e. the field being accessed is the same field */ and ( loc2 is [FieldAccess fa2: loc is [FieldAccess fa: not fa2.field.sourceLocation.null and not fa.field.sourceLocation.null and fa2.field.sourceLocation.startLine == fa.field.sourceLocation.startLine and fa.field is [Field: /* do not match against the lambda generated fields */ name != "~environment" and name != "~method" and name != "prototype" ]* ]] or loc2 is [VariableAccess va2: loc is [VariableAccess va: not va2.variable.sourceLocation.null and not va.variable.sourceLocation.null and va2.variable.sourceLocation.startLine == va.variable.sourceLocation.startLine and not va.this and not va2.this and va.variable is [Variable: not isTemp ]* ]] ) /* FieldAccess outside of lambda that isn't another assignment */ and not loc2 in [AssignmentStatement: lhs.location is [Location: transitiveBase === loc2.transitiveBase]] and not loc2.sourceLocation.null and not fc.sourceLocation.null and loc2.sourceLocation.startLine > fc.sourceLocation.startLine ]*
]* ]]*] ]

StructuralRule.Notes:
Ideally we should flag on options passed to a template function. However, the template function is just a function returned by a call to Handlebars.compile of Handlebars.precompile. Unfortunately, in order for SCA to understand hardcoded templates, it completely transforms this code, completely removing the original calls to compile/precompile. Therefore we're unable to reliably determine the function call taking the parameter, and instead try to just determine the assignment of the original option, rather than when it is used in the template.
This rule is for flagging when protoype resolution is allowed by default. Please note: particularly dangerous allowed unless explicitly allowed with a different property. Rule DBCF5E6D-C7DC-49D4-8158-95F7AAE15614 is for flagging that scenario.
StructuralRule.Predicate: FieldAccess fa: fa.field.name matches "allowProtoMethodsByDefault|allowProtoPropertiesByDefault" and fa in [AssignmentStatement: lhs.location is [Location l: l.transitiveBase === fa.transitiveBase ] and rhs.constantValue == true ]

StructuralRule.Notes:
Ideally we should flag on options passed to a template function. However, the template function is just a function returned by a call to Handlebars.compile of Handlebars.precompile. Unfortunately, in order for SCA to understand hardcoded templates, it completely transforms this code, completely removing the original calls to compile/precompile. Therefore we're unable to reliably determine the function call taking the parameter, and instead try to just determine the assignment of the original option, rather than when it is used in the template.
There are 2 versions of this rule. - 1 for allowing particularly dangerous properties, - 1 that just allows any properties.
This is the one allowing ANY properties/methods.

CharacterizationRule.Notes: _.partition(array, predicate); Returns an array of 2 arrays, effectively splitting "array" into 2, one whose elements return true from the predicate function and the other where the elements return false The array is passed to predicate one value at a time, but the value returned from the callback is not something that's tainted, it's a boolean value. So we need both a Calls and a passthru on this.

React.createElement() is translated to an instantiation of the element with properties set: __reactRefObject - refers arg1 children - refers to arg2
In the case that createElement is passed a known value, the type of the object will be created from that i.e. createElement('div', ...) translates to a HTMLDivElement.

So we basically have to reverse back up from createElement(2), to finding the place the array is accessed and the untrusted element assigned. This allows us to check that the type of element has been created through JSON.parse(), similar to the sink on __reactRefObject.

Defect 30725 - Sinks on object fields when passed to parameter in JS The rule would trigger if any tainted data is passed in the object passed to the tag as opposed to when only 'to' is tainted.

where variable 'pathto' is derived from not validated user input

CharacterizationRule.Notes:
Attempts to cleanse the 'content' field access when the corresponding 'role' is not 'system'. Example: const chatCompletion = await openai.chat.completions.create({ messages: [ { role: 'system', content: 'be helpful' }, { role: 'user', content: user_input() }, ], model: 'gpt-3.5-turbo', }); Since the FieldAccess of 'content' is a "Write" and not a "Read", TaintCleanse doesn't work on it. The workaround is to cleanse the rhs instead. The side-effect of this, is when the rhs is a VariableAccess, it will carry +VALIDATED_PROMPT_INJECTION in subsequent reads and won't trigger Prompt Injection sinks when it's used in a system prompt content. However, this is not a common scenario so we'll accept it.
Also, the sourceLocation condition is a workaround for an SCA defect where 2 different anonymous objects are considered as equal by SCA's structural analyzer.
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FieldAccess fa1: name == "content" and enclosingFunction contains [AssignmentStatement: lhs is [FieldAccess fa2: name == "role" and fa1.instance == fa2.instance and fa1.instance.sourceLocation.startLine == fa2.instance.sourceLocation.startLine ] and rhs.constantValue != "system" ] and enclosingStatement is [AssignmentStatement: lhs is fa1 and rhs is [Expression rhs: rhs is [Location:] or rhs is [FunctionCall:] ] ]
FunctionCall fc: possibleTargets contains [Function: name == "create" and enclosingClass.supers contains [Class: name == "Completions" and sourceLocation.filePath contains "openai" ] ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes:
In case the user can control the process, can inherently control the output from the process. This will be of the form: child = require('child_process').execFileSync(userInput); ... console.log(child.stdout.read());
child.stdout and child.stderr are "Readable" objects, so have a "read" function on them. For the non-blocking versions of these APIs, they would typically use on('data', callback), which is handled by a separate generic rule. Unfortunately there doesn't seem to be any more specific way to specify this without type inference, though the occurrence of a "read" function being called against a field called stdout or stderr seems not that likely.
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall call: call.possibleTargets contains [Function f: f.name == "read"] and call.instance is [Location l: l.name matches "stdout|stderr"]

CharacterizationRule.Notes:
The "Runnable" type is necessary because, in a typical LangChain use case, the ML model objects are part of a "chain" which has the type "Runnable". On the other hand, this will lead to FPs because "Runnable" has many descendants that aren't ML models. For example: ``` const chain = promptTemplate.pipe(llmModel).pipe(outputParser) const prompt = promptTemplate.invoke(...) // shouldn't be tainted const llmResult = chain.invoke(...) // should have +ML +XSS taint ``` Both invoke() calls will be matched by this rule, but only the second one should be tainted. The solution is to track the dataflow of the chain creation process, and make this rule only work when the instance object contains actual ML models.
This is done in rulescript 'LangChain_Filter' along with internal rules 00E311FA and 40C5F57A.
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: possibleTargets contains [Function: name matches "call|generate(Prompt)?|invoke|predict(Messages)?|_call|_generate(Cached|Uncached)?|_stream(ResponseChunks|Iterator)" and enclosingClass.supers contains [Class: name == "Runnable" and sourceLocation.filePath contains "@langchain" ] ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Source for: var s = $("#myForm").serialize(); serialize() is used on forms, it can can act on specific form related objects, parts of or entire forms, to serialize them and URL encode them. Technically this might not always be a source (there could be form items that can't be controlled), but since I don't think we can really know this, I'm just going to assume it's a source. There's also a passthrough on this API for when you can control the DOM element that's serialized (since you will very likely then have control over it).
Passthru for: $("img").attr("width", data); attr() for HTML attributes, prop() for DOM properties. data() is for arbitrary object values, this rule is for variant run against a jQuery object

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Entrypoint for jqXHR callbacks. For the successful variants, the first argument is the data returned from the ajax request. For the case of always(), this changes whether it was a success event or not. If failed, because another jqXHR object, which could plausibly cause duplicate issues, but there's nothing we can do about this, it's runtime behaviour.
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function f: name matches "done|always|then|success"] and fc.instance is [Location: name matches "(?i)(jq)?xhr"] and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression lambda: possibleFunctionTargets contains [Function func: func.parameters[0] is [Variable p: ]] ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes:
Handlebars has a helper, including a level. The 'level' is difficult to identify from the SCA translation, so we will not differentiate between debug and other logging levels.
This looks of the form:
{{log message level="info"}}
but is translated to:
~t1 = {} ~t1.level = 'info' tag~options.helpers.log(message, ~t1)
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name == "log"] and fc.instance is [FieldAccess: name == "helpers" and instance is [Location: name == "tag~options"] ] and fc.arguments contains [Expression arg: /* * log takes varargs, but don't want match on options arg at the end * so don't sink on the options that takes the level */ not type.definition.fields contains [Field: name == "level"] ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes:
Handlebars logging is of the form:
Handlebars.logger.log(level, ...message) Handlebars.log(level, ...message) or in a builtin helper:
{{log message level="info"}}
The source code shows: - level is - a string (either 'debug', 'info', 'warn' or 'error') - a number (referring to the index of the array ['debug', 'info', 'warn', 'error']). - If level is set to that index or lower, everything above is shown - message is varargs
The definition files (included with the source and installed with SCA) say: - level is ONLY a number - Handlebars.logger has constants for DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR indicating the level - these are not in the source and show up as undefined - message is a single object - doesn't allow varargs
In the case that you do pass a string that doesn't match any of the following, the code tries to parse it as a number. So if you pass a constant like 'foo' (or undefined if trying to use one of those constants that don't exist), the JS parses this into the special NaN constant, and nothing gets logged!
So the testcases that we can write don't actually compile with TS when importing types properly. Looking back at different verisons of the source, it looks like the definitions are compatible with 3.x (currently at 4.7.7), so the rules will be written to account for both, but the test cases will primarily be written for 4.7.7, as very few customers will be using such an old version (due to security vulnerabilities).

CharacterizationRule.Notes:
In the case that a hardcoded template is used, SCA transforms the code, removing the call to compile/precompile, so rules 7549A8A8-B287-49D9-AC3A-EC43FD07FCE2 and F12FA1EA-65A8-4222-9D8E-C8FC306E2B01 don't match.
In this case however, the options passed to the original compile/precompile call get put onto a noEscape property of a synthetic variable "tag~options". Unfortunately, this is the best we have to go with at the time of authoring.
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: AssignmentStatement as: lhs is [FieldAccess fa: field.name == "noEscape" and instance is [Location: name == "tag~options"] ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes:
Typically if you want to make sure something is not encoded, you will pass it to new Handlebars.SafeString(0) inside a handlebars helper.
All other scenarios should be handled by SCA automatically to go through to actual XSS sinks (e.g. putting it somewhere in the DOM).
If we had conditional passthroughs, we could have this add a specific taint, and then a passthrough for Handlebars.escapeExpression that is conditional on that taint. Alas, we don't have conditional passthroughs, so we instead have to sink on SafeString()
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name == "init^" and enclosingClass is [Class: name == "SafeString" and namespace.name == "Handlebars" ] ] and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression arg: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Octane 1020006 provided Express request type. `csrfToken` function is injected by deprecated middleware csurf. Note: The reason for having a csrfToken is to send it to the client. Therefore, it should be used together with PRIVATE and should not be a PV sink in HTTP headers or response bodies. Only provide limited support for CodeSecurityAdvent 2022 challenge.

Entrypoint for some lambda functions in NodeGoat that can't be matched by A473F20E or 725AB5F6. This rule is very broad so we'll rely on rulescript 'expressjs_duplicated_sources_cleanup' to remove duplicated issues with the other 2 rules.
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: Function: parameters.length > 1 and parameters[0] is [Variable req: name matches "(?i)req(uest)?" and not type.definition is [Class: name == "Request"] ] and parameters[1] is [Variable: name matches "(?i)res(ponse)?"]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: This is formatVersion 16.10 so can specify the individual fields on the entrypoint. The Request object is an extension of the builtin Node.js one, so it also includes the fields from that. Note: included baseUrl as a tainted field, which is set depending on routing, but this can take a type of regular expression string, so if vague enough, could constitute user input Remove "app" conditions when bug 54435 fixed
CharacterizationRule.Definition: foreach p { TaintEntrypoint(p.baseUrl, {+XSS +WEB +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_DOM +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_SELF +VALIDATED_CLIENT_SIDE_TEMPLATE_INJECTION}) TaintEntrypoint(p.body, {+XSS +WEB +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_DOM +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_SELF +VALIDATED_CLIENT_SIDE_TEMPLATE_INJECTION}) TaintEntrypoint(p.cookies, {+XSS +WEB +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_DOM +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_SELF +VALIDATED_CLIENT_SIDE_TEMPLATE_INJECTION}) TaintEntrypoint(p.hostname, {+XSS +WEB +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_DOM +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_SELF +VALIDATED_CLIENT_SIDE_TEMPLATE_INJECTION}) TaintEntrypoint(p.ip, {+NUMBER +WEB +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_DOM +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_SELF +VALIDATED_CLIENT_SIDE_TEMPLATE_INJECTION}) TaintEntrypoint(p.ips, {+NUMBER +WEB +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_DOM +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_SELF +VALIDATED_CLIENT_SIDE_TEMPLATE_INJECTION}) TaintEntrypoint(p.originalUrl, {+XSS +WEB +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_DOM +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_SELF +VALIDATED_CLIENT_SIDE_TEMPLATE_INJECTION}) TaintEntrypoint(p.params, {+XSS +WEB +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_DOM +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_SELF +VALIDATED_CLIENT_SIDE_TEMPLATE_INJECTION}) TaintEntrypoint(p.path, {+XSS +WEB +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_DOM +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_SELF +VALIDATED_CLIENT_SIDE_TEMPLATE_INJECTION}) TaintEntrypoint(p.query, {+XSS +WEB +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_DOM +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_SELF +VALIDATED_CLIENT_SIDE_TEMPLATE_INJECTION}) TaintEntrypoint(p.signedCookies, {+XSS +WEB +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_DOM +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_SELF +VALIDATED_CLIENT_SIDE_TEMPLATE_INJECTION}) TaintEntrypoint(p.subdomains, {+XSS +WEB +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_DOM +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_SELF +VALIDATED_CLIENT_SIDE_TEMPLATE_INJECTION}) TaintEntrypoint(p.headers, {+XSS +WEB +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_DOM +VALIDATED_CROSS_SITE_SCRIPTING_SELF +VALIDATED_CLIENT_SIDE_TEMPLATE_INJECTION}) CharacterizationRule.Notes:
Attempts to attach a +SYSTEM_PROMPT flag on the assignment to FieldAccess named 'system', so the Prompt Injection sink rule can require this flag to ensure we only sink on system prompts. Example: client.messages.create({ max_tokens: 1024, messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Hello, Claude' }], model: 'claude-3-haiku-20240307', system: tainted_source(), }); Since TaintCleanse can only apply to READs, we have to cleanse the rhs, which has a side effect when the rhs is a Location and it's used again as a prompt message, since it still carries +SYSTEM_PROMPT, it will trigger Prompt Injection even if it's only added as user prompt.
This is a less common scenario so we'll accept it for now.
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: AssignmentStatement: lhs is [FieldAccess: name == "system"] and rhs is [Expression rhs: rhs is [Location:] or rhs is [FunctionCall:] ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: The linky filter is i.e. ng-href="foo | linky:'_blank':{attribute: 'value'}" is translated as going through a function "linkyFilter" where the 0th argument is the input, the 1st argument is the optional "window" and the 2nd argument is other attributes that may go on an <a> element. As far as I can tell the 1st and 2nd argument aren't actually vulnerable to anything apart from PV/SIL (they check for quotes when dynamically creating the <a> tag and also do sanitization afterwards to remove any inline JS or attributes that create events such as onmouseover). For the 0th argument we don't flag PV/SIL, since this will flag on the eventual sink of say ngHref after going through the passthrough. Can also be called as $filter("linky")(foo, '_blank', {attribute: 'value'}), but we currently have no way of writing a rule to identify the function returned from a function call (bug 53263)
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: possibleTargets contains [Function: name == "linkyFilter"] and fc.arguments contains [Expression arg: arg != fc.arguments[0]]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: The linky filter is i.e. {{ foo | linky }} is translated as going through a function "linkyFilter", so need a passthrough for the linky filter in order for the taint to continue through to the sink. Can also be called as $filter("linky")(foo), but we currently have no way of writing a rule to identify the function returned from a function call (bug 53263)
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: possibleTargets contains [Function: name == "linkyFilter"] and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression arg: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Legacy version of promises in Angular used success(callback) and error(callback) instead of then(successCallback, errorCallback). There are also "finally()" and "catch()" variants that are now obsolete. These are used in the "juiceshop" project for example. Unfortunately we can't really use possibleHeapPaths, since it would require recognizing everything that returns a promise, and even then it's probably not going to be that accurate. There's also deferring of promises, which would lead to no real possibleHeapPaths being present
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name matches "success|error|finally|catch"] and fc.arguments.length == 1 and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression lambda: ] and fc.instance is [Expression this: ] and fc.enclosingStatement is [Statement stmt: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Source for $location.url() and $location.absUrl(); absUrl() includes host/port/scheme, url() returns everything after this. Using the setter variants changes the URL in the browser, but doesn't create a page reload, $window.location.href would be used for this instead. We could plausibly create a Open Redirect sink on the url() getter, but it's mostly harmless as a page reload of the URI would need to be forced some other way.
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function f: f.name matches "absUrl|url" and f.possibleHeapPaths contains "$location"] and fc.arguments.length == 0

CharacterizationRule.Notes: getter variant of $location.search()
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function f: f.name == "search" and f.possibleHeapPaths contains "$location"] and (fc.arguments.length == 0 or fc.arguments.length == 1)

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Sinks for orderByFilter, takes an optional expression as the 1st argument, which can be a string, function or an array of functions. Will be evaluated at the time with the current scope, similar to $eval() The filter "filter" does the same as well.
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name matches "(orderBy|filter)Filter"] and fc.arguments[1] is [Expression inArg: ]
FunctionCall fc: possibleTargets contains [Function: name == "trustAsHtml" and possibleHeapPaths contains "$sce"] and arguments[0] is [Expression e: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: angular.extend takes a destination object and one or more source objects from which to copy enumerable properties Then returns a reference to the destination (so also taint from src -> return). angular.merge does the same, except it performs a deep copy by recursively descending into object properties
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function f: name matches "extend|merge" and f.possibleHeapPaths contains "angular"] and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression dest: ] and fc.arguments contains [Expression src: src != fc.arguments[0]]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: setter variant of $location.search()
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function f: f.name == "search" and f.possibleHeapPaths contains "$location"] and fc.arguments.length == 2 and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression key: ] and fc.arguments[1] is [Expression inArg: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: $interval() is angular's wrapper for window.setInterval(), except it only takes a function, not a string to evaluate (thus no dynamic code eval) Similarly $timeout is angular's wrapper for window.setTimeout(), but only takes a function, and returns a promise.
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function f: name matches "\$interval|\$timeout"] and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression lambda: ] and fc.enclosingStatement is [Statement stmt: ]

FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name matches "\$watch(Group|Collection)?"] and fc.arguments.length > 1 and fc.arguments[1] is [Expression lambda: ] and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression arg0: ] and fc.instance is [Expression this: ] and fc.enclosingStatement is [Statement stmt: ]
FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name matches "__AngularJSInterpolation|ngBind"] and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression arg: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Calls rules for $injector service
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name matches "instantiate|annotate" and possibleHeapPaths contains "$injector"] and fc.arguments.length == 1 and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression lambda: ] and fc.enclosingStatement is [Statement stmt: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Calls rule for $resource functions when taking multiple arguments
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function f: f.name matches "get|save|query|remove|delete"] and fc.instance.possibleHeapPaths contains "$resource" and fc.arguments.length == 2 and fc.arguments[1] is [Expression lambda: ] and fc.enclosingStatement is [Statement stmt: ]
FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function f: name == "$q"] and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression lambda: ] and fc.enclosingStatement is [Statement stmt: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Source for $location.url() and $location.absUrl(); absUrl() includes host/port/scheme, url() returns everything after this. Using the setter variants changes the URL in the browser, but doesn't create a page reload, $window.location.href would be used for this instead. We could plausibly create a Open Redirect sink on the url() getter, but it's mostly harmless as a page reload of the URI would need to be forced some other way.
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function f: f.name matches "absUrl|url" and f.possibleHeapPaths contains "$location"] and fc.arguments.length == 0

CharacterizationRule.Notes: $interval() is angular's wrapper for window.setInterval(), except it only takes a function, not a string to evaluate (thus no dynamic code eval) Similarly $timeout is angular's wrapper for window.setTimeout(), but only takes a function, and returns a promise.
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function f: name matches "\$interval|\$timeout"] and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression lambda: ] and fc.enclosingStatement is [Statement stmt: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Variant specifying the _this_
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function f: name == "forEach" and f.possibleHeapPaths contains "angular"] and fc.arguments.length == 3 and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression arg: ] and fc.arguments[1] is [Expression lambda: ] and fc.enclosingStatement is [Statement stmt: ] and fc.arguments[2] is [Expression this: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: angular.forEach either takes 2 args where the latter is the lambda, or 3 args where the last is the _this_
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function f: name == "forEach" and f.possibleHeapPaths contains "angular"] and fc.arguments.length == 2 and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression arg: ] and fc.arguments[1] is [Expression lambda: ] and fc.enclosingStatement is [Statement stmt: ] and fc.instance is [Expression this: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: angular.extend takes a destination object and one or more source objects from which to copy enumerable properties Then returns a reference to the destination (so also taint from src -> return). angular.merge does the same, except it performs a deep copy by recursively descending into object properties
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function f: name matches "extend|merge" and f.possibleHeapPaths contains "angular"] and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression dest: ] and fc.arguments contains [Expression src: src != fc.arguments[0]]

CharacterizationRule.Notes:
This is sometimes used in order to mix markup languages instead of just using Angular expressions. The docs even recommend against this because the embedding template language won't safely escape Angular expressions, leading to XSS.
This rule will flag when a user can control the start/end symbols set for the expression. Whereas they may have previously only been able to place data into some place benign, this may lead to being able to create an XSS.

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Legacy version of promises in Angular used success(callback) and error(callback) instead of then(successCallback, errorCallback). There are also "finally()" and "catch()" variants that are now obsolete. These are used in the "juiceshop" project for example. Unfortunately we can't really use possibleHeapPaths, since it would require recognizing everything that returns a promise, and even then it's probably not going to be that accurate. There's also deferring of promises, which would lead to no real possibleHeapPaths being present
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name matches "error|catch"] and fc.arguments.length == 1 and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression lambda: lambda.possibleFunctionTargets contains [Function: parameters.length == 1 and parameters[0] is [Variable v: ] ] ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Legacy version of promises in Angular used success(callback) and error(callback) instead of then(successCallback, errorCallback). There are also "finally()" and "catch()" variants that are now obsolete. These are used in the "juiceshop" project for example. Unfortunately we can't really use possibleHeapPaths, since it would require recognizing everything that returns a promise, and even then it's probably not going to be that accurate. There's also deferring of promises, which would lead to no real possibleHeapPaths being present
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name matches "error|catch"] and fc.arguments.length == 1 and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression lambda: lambda.possibleFunctionTargets contains [Function: parameters.length == 1 and parameters[0] is [Variable v: ] ] ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Legacy version of promises in Angular used success(callback) and error(callback) instead of then(successCallback, errorCallback). There are also "finally()" and "catch()" variants that are now obsolete. These are used in the "juiceshop" project for example. Unfortunately we can't really use possibleHeapPaths, since it would require recognizing everything that returns a promise, and even then it's probably not going to be that accurate. There's also deferring of promises, which would lead to no real possibleHeapPaths being present
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name matches "success|error|finally|catch"] and fc.arguments.length == 1 and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression lambda: ] and fc.instance is [Expression this: ] and fc.enclosingStatement is [Statement stmt: ]

FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name == "then"] and fc.arguments.length == 2 and fc.arguments[1] is [Expression lambda: lambda.possibleFunctionTargets contains [Function: parameters[0] is [Variable v: ] ] ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Calls rules for JS promises with then(success, failure). Where each callback can be passed the instance of the call.
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name == "then"] /* can take one or two args */ and fc.arguments.length < 3 and fc.enclosingStatement is [Statement stmt: ] and fc.instance is [Expression this: ] and fc.arguments contains [Expression lambda: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Calls rules for $injector service
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name matches "instantiate|annotate" and possibleHeapPaths contains "$injector"] and fc.arguments.length == 1 and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression lambda: ] and fc.enclosingStatement is [Statement stmt: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Calls rules for $injector.invoke() when _not_ specifying an instance
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name == "invoke" and possibleHeapPaths contains "$injector"] and fc.arguments.length == 1 and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression lambda: ] and fc.enclosingStatement is [Statement stmt: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Calls rules for $injector.invoke() when specifying an instance
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name == "invoke" and possibleHeapPaths contains "$injector"] and fc.arguments.length > 1 and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression lambda: ] and fc.arguments[1] is [Expression this: ] and fc.enclosingStatement is [Statement stmt: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: This is for @angular/router.ParamMap: https://angular.io/api/router/ParamMap Don't usually have type info available due to use in Observable. Therefore don't currently check instance type. There is also a get() function, but that is covered by another general rule for Maps.
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name == "getAll"] and fc.arguments.length == 1 and fc.instance is [Expression this: ]
FieldAccess fa: fa.field.name matches "queryParams|queryParamMap" and instance.possibleTypes contains [Type: name matches "(@angular/router\.)?ActivatedRoute(Snapshot)?"]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: sources for hash|href|search getters. Can be field or function depending on whether source resolved.
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FieldAccess fa: fa.field.name matches "hash|href|search" and instance.possibleTypes contains [Type: name matches "(@angular/common\.)?PlatformLocation"]

CharacterizationRule.Notes:
For API onUrlChange(fn: (url: string, state: unknown) => void)
Can't assume state is tainted, but can assume 'url' is.

For API onUrlChange(fn: (url: string, state: unknown) => void)
Can't assume state is tainted, but can assume 'url' is.
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function f: f.name == "onUrlChange" ] and fc.arguments.length == 1 and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression lambda: ] and fc.instance is [Expression this: ] and fc.enclosingStatement is [Statement stmt: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Location.stripTrailingSlash() (static) passthrough. Strips the trailing slash. Is smart enough to strip trailing slash prior to # or ?
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name == "stripTrailingSlash" ] and fc.instance is [Location: name matches "Location(_2)?"] and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression arg: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Location.joinWithSlash() (static) passthrough. Concatenates 2 strings with a slash if there isn't one.
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name == "joinWithSlash" ] and fc.instance is [Location: name matches "Location(_2)?"] and fc.arguments contains [Expression arg: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Location.normalizeQueryParams() (static) passthrough. Mainly just prepends '#' if there isn't one
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name == "normalizeQueryParams" ] and fc.instance is [Location: name matches "Location(_2)?"] and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression arg: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Location.prepareExternalUrl() passthrough
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name == "prepareExternalUrl" ] and fc.instance.possibleTypes contains [Type: name matches "(@angular/common\.)?Location(_2)?"] and fc.arguments[0] is [Expression arg: ]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: Location.path() source. If it takes a "true" argument, it includes the hash, which is HTML encoded on top of Angular's protections.
CharacterizationRule.StructuralMatch: FunctionCall fc: fc.possibleTargets contains [Function: name == "path" ] and fc.instance.possibleTypes contains [Type: name matches "(@angular/common\.)?Location(_2)?"] and fc.arguments.length > 0 and fc.arguments[0] is [BooleanLiteral: value is true]

CharacterizationRule.Notes: SlicePipe passthrough

CharacterizationRule.Notes: The "currency", which is supposed to be a string, is effectively just any plaintext string passed straight along prior to the number This is the passthrough for the CurrencyPipe, which allows the same thing

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>The method <Replace key="EnclosingFunction.name"/> on line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/> accesses an Azure Queue/Blob with an attacker-controlled value and without proper access control, thereby allowing the attacker to perform unauthorized functions.<AltParagraph>Accessing an Azure Queue/Blob with a user-controlled value and without proper access control may allow an attacker to view/modify/delete unauthorized Queue/Blob and its messages/contents.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Recommendations: Do not allow untrusted data to control sensitive values. In many cases where this error occurs, the application expects a particular input, which is specific to user/program. If possible, instead of relying on the input to remain within an expected range, the application should guarantee reasonable behavior by using the input only to select from a predetermined set of safe values. If the input is maliciously crafted, the value passed to the sensitive function should default to some safe selection from this set. Even if the set of safe values cannot be known in advance, it is often possible to validate that the input falls within some safe range of values. If neither of these forms of validation is possible, you may have to redesign the application to avoid the need to accept potentially dangerous values from the user/program.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>Without proper access control, the method <Replace key="EnclosingFunction.name"/> in <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/> can execute a SQL statement on line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> that contains an attacker-controlled primary key, thereby allowing the attacker to access unauthorized records.<AltParagraph>Without proper access control, executing a SQL statement that contains a user-controlled primary key can allow an attacker to view unauthorized records.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Database access control errors occur when: 1. Data enters a program from an untrusted source. In this case, the data enters at in on line . 2. The data is used to specify the value of a primary key in a SQL query. In this case, the data is used by in on line . Example 1: The following code uses a parameterized statement, which escapes metacharacters and prevents SQL injection vulnerabilities, to construct and execute a SQL query that searches for an invoice matching the specified identifier [1]. The identifier is selected from a list of all invoices associated with the current authenticated user. 
	...
	var id = document.form.invoiceID.value;
	var query = "SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = ?";
	db.transaction(function (tx) {
		tx.executeSql(query,[id]);
		}
	)
	...
The problem is that the developer has failed to consider all of the possible values of id. Although the interface generates a list of invoice identifiers that belong to the current user, an attacker might bypass this interface to request any desired invoice. Because the code in this example does not check to ensure that the user has permission to access the requested invoice, it will display any invoice, even if it does not belong to the current user.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>The call to <Replace key="PrimaryCall.name"/> in <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/> on line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> allows JavaScript to be an allowed protocol, which may lead to cross-site scripting vulnerabilities.<AltParagraph>The application allows JavaScript as an allowed protocol, which may lead to cross-site scripting vulnerabilities.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Recommendations: There is very little reason for inline JavaScript in this manner, so JavaScript should not be allowed to run inline where it is by default prevented. There are usually cleaner and more secure ways to run the same functionality, without opening potential security holes within the application.

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | AngularJS Misconfiguration: Dangerous Protocol Allowed

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>The call to <Replace key="PrimaryCall.name"/> in <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/> on line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> disables Strict Contextual Escaping in AngularJS 1, potentially leading to multiple vulnerabilities including cross-site scripting attacks.<AltParagraph>Strict Contextual Escaping is disabled in the AngularJS 1 application, potentially leading to multiple new vulnerabilities.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Recommendations: Avoid disabling this protection mechanism. There is very little overhead within the framework for including this protection, and the only way you could safely decide this should be turned off would be if you are sure that 100% of the site is secure against vulnerabilities, which if this were the case it would likely be a very simple application with no user input.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>The method <Replace key="EnclosingFunction.name"/> in <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/> calls <Replace key="PrimaryCall.name"/> with a command built from untrusted data. This call can cause the program to execute malicious commands on behalf of an attacker.<AltParagraph>Executing commands from an untrusted source or in an untrusted environment can cause an application to execute malicious commands on behalf of an attacker.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Recommendations:
Do not allow users to have direct control over the commands executed by the program. In cases where user input must affect the command to be run, use the input only to make a selection from a predetermined set of safe commands. If the input appears to be malicious, the value passed to the command execution function should either default to some safe selection from this set or the program should decline to execute any command at all.
In cases where user input must be used as an argument to a command executed by the program, this approach often becomes impractical because the set of legitimate argument values is too large or too hard to keep track of. Developers often fall back on implementing a deny list in these situations. A deny list is used to selectively reject or escape potentially dangerous characters before using the input. Any list of unsafe characters is likely to be incomplete and will be heavily dependent on the system where the commands are executed. A better approach is to create a list of characters that are permitted to appear in the input and accept input composed exclusively of characters in the approved set.
An attacker may indirectly control commands executed by a program by modifying the environment in which they are executed. The environment should not be trusted and precautions should be taken to prevent an attacker from using some manipulation of the environment to perform an attack. Whenever possible, commands should be controlled by the application and executed using an absolute path. In cases where the path is not known at compile time, such as for cross-platform applications, an absolute path should be constructed from trusted values during execution. Command values and paths read from configuration files or the environment should be sanity-checked against a set of invariants that define valid values.
Other checks can sometimes be performed to detect if these sources may have been tampered with. For example, if a configuration file is world-writable, the program might refuse to run. In cases where information about the binary to be executed is known in advance, the program may perform checks to verify the identity of the binary. If a binary should always be owned by a particular user or have a particular set of access permissions assigned to it, these properties can be verified programmatically before the binary is executed.
Although it may be impossible to completely protect a program from an imaginative attacker bent on controlling the commands the program executes, be sure to apply the principle of least privilege wherever the program executes an external command: do not hold privileges that are not essential to the execution of the command.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>The method <Replace key="EnclosingFunction.name"/> in <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/> calls <Replace key="PrimaryCall.name"/> to execute a command. This call might allow an attacker to inject malicious commands.<AltParagraph>Executing commands that include unvalidated user input can cause an application to execute malicious commands on behalf of an attacker.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Command injection vulnerabilities take two forms: - An attacker can change the command that the program executes: the attacker explicitly controls what the command is. - An attacker can change the environment in which the command executes: the attacker implicitly controls what the command means. In this case, we are primarily concerned with the second scenario, the possibility that an attacker may be able to change the meaning of the command by changing an environment variable or by putting a malicious executable early in the search path. Command injection vulnerabilities of this type occur when: 1. An attacker modifies an application's environment. 2. The application executes a command without specifying an absolute path or verifying the binary being executed. In this case, the command is executed by in on line . 3. By executing the command, the application gives an attacker a privilege or capability that the attacker would not otherwise have. Example 1: The following code is from a web application that provides an interface through which users can update their password on the system. Part of the process for updating passwords in certain network environments is to run a make command in the /var/yp directory. 
...
require('child_process').exec("make", function(error, stdout, stderr){
  ...
});
...
The problem here is that the program does not specify an absolute path for make and fails to clean its environment prior to executing the call to child_process.exec(). If an attacker can modify the $PATH variable to point to a malicious binary called make and then execute the application in their environment, the malicious binary will be loaded instead of the one intended. Because of the nature of the application, it runs with the privileges necessary to perform system operations, which means the attacker's make will now be run with these privileges, possibly giving them complete control of the system.
Description.Recommendations:
An attacker may indirectly control commands executed by a program by modifying the environment in which they are executed. The environment should not be trusted and precautions should be taken to prevent an attacker from using some manipulation of the environment to perform an attack. Whenever possible, commands should be controlled by the application and executed using an absolute path. In cases where the path is not known at compile time, such as for cross-platform applications, an absolute path should be constructed from trusted values during execution. Command values and paths read from configuration files or the environment should be sanity-checked against a set of invariants that define valid values.
Other checks can sometimes be performed to detect if these sources may have been tampered with. For example, if a configuration file is world-writable, the program might refuse to run. In cases where information about the binary to be executed is known in advance, the program may perform checks to verify the identity of the binary. If a binary should always be owned by a particular user or have a particular set of access permissions assigned to it, these properties can be verified programmatically before the binary is executed.
In the end it may be impossible for a program to fully protect itself from an imaginative attacker bent on controlling the commands the program executes. You should strive to identify and protect against every conceivable manipulation of input values and the environment. The goal should be to shut down as many attack vectors as possible.

Tips.Tip: On Windows, the reported issue is not a concern if the command being executed is a Windows internal command. The internal commands do not reside on disk. Instead, they reside in COMMAND.COM, which loads into memory when the computer system is started. A list of internal commands includes: BREAK, CALL, CHCP, CHDIR(CD), CLS, COPY, CTTY, DATE, DEL(ERASE), DIR, ECHO, EXIT, FOR, GOTO, IF, MKDIR(MD), PATH, PAUSE, PROMPT, REM, RENAME(REN), RMDIR(RD), SET, SHIFT, TIME, TYPE, VER, VERIFY, VOL. For an up-to-date list of internal commands specific to your system, consult your system's documentation.

Description.Abstract: A cookie is created without the Secure flag set to true.
Description.Explanation:
Modern web browsers support a Secure flag for each cookie. If the flag is set, the browser will only send the cookie over HTTPS. Sending cookies over an unencrypted channel can expose them to network sniffing attacks, so the secure flag helps keep a cookie's value confidential. This is especially important if the cookie contains private data or carries a session identifier. In this case a cookie is created in in on line , but the Secure property is not set to true. Example 1: In the following example, a cookie is added to the response without setting the Secure property to true. 
  res.cookie('important_cookie', info, {domain: 'secure.example.com', path: '/admin', httpOnly: true, secure: false});
If your application uses both HTTPS and HTTP but does not set the Secure flag, cookies sent during an HTTPS request will also be sent during subsequent HTTP requests. Sniffing network traffic over unencrypted wireless connections is a trivial task for attackers, so sending cookies (especially those with session IDs) over HTTP can result in application compromise.
Description.Recommendations:
Set the Secure flag on all new cookies to instruct browsers not to send these cookies in the clear. Example 2: 
	res.cookie('important_cookie', info, {domain: 'secure.example.com', path: '/admin', httpOnly: true, secure: true});

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Cookie Security: Cookie not Sent Over SSL

Description.Abstract: The program creates a cookie in on line , but fails to set the HttpOnly flag to true.The program creates a cookie, but fails to set the HttpOnly flag to true.
Description.Explanation:
All major browsers support the HttpOnly cookie property to prevent client-side scripts from accessing the cookie. Cross-site scripting attacks often access cookies in an attempt to steal session identifiers or authentication tokens. Without the HttpOnly flag enabled, attackers have easier access to user cookies. In this case, a cookie is set in in on line , but the HttpOnly flag is not set or is set to false. Example 1: The following code creates a cookie without setting the httpOnly property. 
  res.cookie('important_cookie', info, {domain: 'secure.example.com', path: '/admin'});
Description.Recommendations:
Enable the HttpOnly property when you create cookies. Example 2: The following code creates the same cookie as the code in Example 1, but this example sets the httpOnly property to true. 
res.cookie('important_cookie', info, {domain: 'secure.example.com', path: '/admin', httpOnly: true});
Several mechanisms to bypass the setting of HttpOnly to true have been developed, and therefore it is not completely effective.

Reference.Title: Round-up: Ways to bypass HttpOnly (and HTTP Basic auth)
Reference.Author: Amit Klein

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Cookie Security: HTTPOnly not Set

Description.Abstract: The program fails to set the SameSite attribute on session cookies.
Description.Explanation:
Browsers automatically append cookies to every HTTP request made to the site that sets the cookie. Cookies might store sensitive data such as session ID and authorization token or site data that is shared between different requests to the same site during a session. An attacker can perform an impersonation attack by generating a request to the authenticated site from a third-party site page loaded on the client machine because the browser automatically appends the cookie to the request. The SameSite attribute limits the scope of the cookie so that it is only attached to a request if the request is generated from first-party or same-site context. This helps to protect cookies from Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks. The SameSite attribute can have the following three values: - Strict: When set to Strict, cookies are only sent along with requests upon top-level navigation. - Lax: When set to Lax, cookies are sent with top-level navigation from the same host as well as GET requests originating from third-party sites, including those that have either iframe or href tags that link to the host site. For example, suppose there is a third-party site that has either iframe or href tags that link to the host site. If a user follows the link, the request will include the cookie. - None: Cookies are sent in all requests made to the site within the path and domain scope set for the cookie. Requests generated due to form submissions using the POST method are also allowed to send cookies with the request. In this case, the SameSite property is set to None, false, or is omitted in on line . Example 1: The following code disables the SameSite attribute for session cookies. 
app.get('/', function (req, res) {
    ...
    res.cookie('name', 'Foo', { sameSite: false });
    ...
}

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Cookie Security: Missing SameSite Attribute

Description.Abstract: A cookie with an overly broad domain opens an application to attack through other applications.
Description.Explanation:
Developers often set cookies to be active across a base domain such as ".example.com". This exposes the cookie to all web applications on the base domain and any sub-domains. Because cookies often carry sensitive information such as session identifiers, sharing cookies across applications can cause a vulnerability in one application to compromise another application. Example 1: Suppose you have a secure application deployed at http://secure.example.com/ and the application sets a session ID cookie with the domain ".example.com" when a user logs in. For example: 
  cookie_options = {};
  cookie_options.domain = '.example.com';
  ...
  res.cookie('important_cookie', info, cookie_options);
Suppose you have another, less secure, application at http://insecure.example.com/, and it contains a cross-site scripting vulnerability. Any user authenticated to http://secure.example.com that browses to http://insecure.example.com risks exposing their session cookie from http://secure.example.com. In addition to reading a cookie, it might be possible for attackers to perform a Cookie Poisoning attack by using insecure.example.com to create its own overly broad cookie that overwrites the cookie from secure.example.com.

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Cookie Security: Overly Broad Domain

Description.Abstract: A cookie with an overly broad path can be accessed through other applications on the same domain.
Description.Explanation:
Developers often set cookies to be accessible from the root context path ("/"). This exposes the cookie to all web applications on the domain. Because cookies often carry sensitive information such as session identifiers, sharing cookies across applications can cause a vulnerability in one application to compromise another application. Example 1: Imagine you have a forum application deployed at http://communitypages.example.com/MyForum and the application sets a session ID cookie with the path "/" when users log in to the forum. For example: 
  cookie_options = {};
  cookie_options.path = '/';
  ...
  res.cookie('important_cookie', info, cookie_options);
Suppose an attacker creates another application at http://communitypages.example.com/EvilSite and posts a link to this site on the forum. When a user of the forum clicks this link, the browser will send the cookie set by /MyForum to the application running at /EvilSite. By stealing the session ID, the attacker can compromise the account of any forum user that browsed to /EvilSite. In addition to reading a cookie, it might be possible for attackers to perform a Cookie Poisoning attack by using /EvilSite to create its own overly broad cookie that overwrites the cookie from /MyForum.

Description.Abstract: The SameSite attribute on session cookies is not set to Strict.
Description.Explanation:
The SameSite attribute protects cookies from attacks such as Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF). Session cookies represent a user to the site so that the user can perform authorized actions. However, the browser automatically sends the cookies with the request and therefore users and web sites implicitly trust the browser for authorization. An attacker can misuse this trust and make a request to the site on behalf of the user by embedding links inside the href and src attribute of tags such as link and iframe in third-party site pages that an attacker controls. If an attacker is able to lure an unsuspecting user to the third-party site that they control, the attacker can make requests that automatically include the session cookie authorizing the user, effectively authorizing the attacker as if they were the user. Set the value of the SameSite attribute to Strict in session cookies. This restricts the browser to append cookies only to requests that are either top-level navigation or originate from the same site. Requests that originate from third-party sites via links in various tags such as iframe, img, and form do not have these cookies and therefore prevent the site from taking action that the user might not have authorized. In this case, the SameSite attribute is set to Lax in on line . Example 1: The following code sets the value of the SameSite attribute to Lax for session cookies. 
app.get('/', function (req, res) {
    ...
    res.cookie('name', 'Foo', { sameSite: "Lax" });
    ...
}

Reference.Title: Fortify Taxonomy | Cookie Security: Overly Permissive SameSite Attribute

Description.Abstract: Failure to restrict inclusion of an application within an iframe can lead to cross-site request forgery or phishing attacks.
Description.Explanation: Cross-frame scripting vulnerabilities occur when an application: 1. Allows itself to be included inside an iframe. 2. Fails to specify framing policy via the X-Frame-Options header. 3. Uses poor protection, such as JavaScript-based frame busting logic. Cross-frame scripting vulnerabilities often form the basis of clickjacking exploits that attackers may use to conduct cross-site request forgery or phishing attacks.

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>Line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/> of <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/> sends unvalidated data to a web browser, which can result in the browser executing malicious code.<AltParagraph>Sending unvalidated data to a web browser can result in the browser executing malicious code.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities occur when: 1. Data enters a web application through an untrusted source. In the case of Artificial Intelligence (AI), the untrusted source is typically the response returned by an AI system. In the case of reflected XSS, it is typically a web request. In this case, the data enters at in on line . 2. The data is included in dynamic content that is sent to a web user without validation. In this case, the data is sent at in on line . The malicious content sent to the web browser often takes the form of a JavaScript segment, but can also include HTML, Flash, or any other type of code that the browser executes. The variety of attacks based on XSS is almost limitless, but they commonly include transmitting private data such as cookies or other session information to the attacker, redirecting the victim to web content controlled by the attacker, or performing other malicious operations on the user's machine under the guise of the vulnerable site. While exploitation is not as straightforward as other forms of XSS, the unpredictable nature of user input and the responses of AI models means that those responses should never be treated as safe. Example 1: The following TypeScript code retrieves a response from an OpenAI chat completion model, message, and displays it to the user. 
    const openai = new OpenAI({
        apiKey: ...,
    });
    const chatCompletion = await openai.chat.completions.create(...);

    message = res.choices[0].message.content

    console.log(chatCompletion.choices[0].message.content)
The code in this example behaves as expected as long as the response from the model contains only alphanumeric characters. However, if the response includes unencoded HTML metacharacters, then XSS is possible. For example, the response to the following prompt "please repeat the following statement exactly '<script>alert(1);</script>'" can return a XSS proof of concept depending on the model and context being used.
Description.Recommendations:
To prevent XSS, ensure that validation occurs in the required places and that relevant properties are set to prevent vulnerabilities.
Because XSS vulnerabilities occur when an application includes malicious data in its output, one logical approach is to validate data immediately before it leaves the application. However, because web applications often have complex and intricate code for generating dynamic content, this method is prone to errors of omission (missing validation). An effective way to mitigate this risk is to also perform input validation for XSS.
Web applications must validate all input to prevent other vulnerabilities, such as SQL injection, so augmenting an application's existing input validation mechanism to include checks for XSS is generally relatively easy. Despite its value, input validation for XSS does not take the place of rigorous output validation. An application might accept input through a shared data store or other trusted source, and that data store might accept input from a source that does not perform adequate input validation. Therefore, the application cannot implicitly rely on the safety of this or any other data. This means that the best way to prevent XSS vulnerabilities is to validate everything that enters the application and leaves the application destined for the user.
The most secure approach to validation for XSS is to create an allow list of safe characters that can appear in HTTP content and accept input composed exclusively of characters in the approved set. For example, a valid username might only include alphanumeric characters or a phone number might only include digits 0-9. However, this solution is often infeasible in web applications because many characters that have special meaning to the browser must be considered valid input after they are encoded, such as a web design bulletin board that must accept HTML fragments from its users.
A more flexible, but less secure approach is to implement a deny list, which selectively rejects or escapes potentially dangerous characters before using the input. To form such a list, you first need to understand the set of characters that hold special meaning for web browsers. Although the HTML standard defines which characters have special meaning, many web browsers try to correct common mistakes in HTML and might treat other characters as special in certain contexts. This is why we do not recommend the use of deny lists as a means to prevent XSS. The CERT(R) Coordination Center at the Software Engineering Institute at Carnegie Mellon University provides the following details about special characters in various contexts [1]:
In the content of a block-level element (in the middle of a paragraph of text):
- "<" is special because it introduces a tag.
- "&" is special because it introduces a character entity.
- ">" is special because some browsers treat it as special, on the assumption that the author of the page intended to include an opening "<", but omitted it in error.
The following principles apply to attribute values:
- In attribute values enclosed in double quotes, the double quotes are special because they mark the end of the attribute value.
- In attribute values enclosed in single quotes, the single quotes are special because they mark the end of the attribute value.
- In attribute values without any quotes, white-space characters, such as space and tab, are special.
- "&" is special when used with certain attributes, because it introduces a character entity.
In URLs, for example, a search engine might provide a link within the results page that the user can click to re-run the search. This can be implemented by encoding the search query inside the URL, which introduces additional special characters:
- Space, tab, and new line are special because they mark the end of the URL.
- "&" is special because it either introduces a character entity or separates CGI parameters.
- Non-ASCII characters (that is, everything greater than 127 in the ISO-8859-1 encoding) are not allowed in URLs, so they are considered to be special in this context.
- The "%" symbol must be filtered from input anywhere parameters encoded with HTTP escape sequences are decoded by server-side code. For example, "%" must be filtered if input such as "%68%65%6C%6C%6F" becomes "hello" when it appears on the web page.
Within the body of a <SCRIPT> </SCRIPT>:
- Filter out semicolons, parentheses, braces, and newline characters in situations where text can be inserted directly into a pre-existing script tag.
Server-side scripts:
- Server-side scripts that convert any exclamation characters (!) in input to double-quote characters (") on output might require additional filtering.
Other possibilities:
- If an attacker submits a request in UTF-7, the special character '<' appears as '+ADw-' and might bypass filtering. If the output is included in a page that does not explicitly specify an encoding format, then some browsers try to intelligently identify the encoding based on the content (in this case, UTF-7).
After you identify the correct points in an application to perform validation for XSS attacks and what special characters the validation should consider, the next challenge is to identify how your validation handles special characters. If special characters are not considered valid input to the application, then you can reject any input that contains special characters as invalid. A second option is to remove special characters with filtering. However, filtering has the side effect of changing any visual representation of the filtered content and might be unacceptable in circumstances where the integrity of the input must be preserved for display.
If input containing special characters must be accepted and displayed accurately, validation must encode any special characters to remove their significance. A complete list of ISO 8859-1 encoded values for special characters is provided as part of the official HTML specification [2].
Many application servers attempt to limit an application's exposure to XSS vulnerabilities by providing implementations for the functions responsible for setting certain specific HTTP response content that perform validation for the characters essential to XSS attacks. Do not rely on the server running your application to make it secure. For any developed application, there are no guarantees about which application servers it will run on during its lifetime. As standards and known exploits evolve, there are no guarantees that application servers will continue to stay in sync.

Reference.Title: Understanding Malicious Content Mitigation for Web Developers

Description.Abstract: <Paragraph>The method <Replace key="EnclosingFunction.name"/> in <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.file"/> sends unvalidated data to a web browser on line <Replace key="PrimaryLocation.line"/>, which can result in the browser executing malicious code.<AltParagraph>Sending unvalidated data to a web browser can result in the browser executing malicious code.</AltParagraph></Paragraph>
Description.Explanation:
Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities occur when: 1. Data enters a web application through an untrusted source. In the case of DOM-based Artificial Intelegence (AI) XSS, data from an AI prompt response is written back into the page with client-side code. In the case of reflected XSS, the untrusted source is typically a web request, while in the case of persisted (also known as stored) XSS it is typically a database or other back-end data store. In this case, the data enters at in on line . 2. The data is included in dynamic content that is sent to a web user without validation. In the case of DOM-based XSS, malicious content is executed as part of DOM (Document Object Model) creation, whenever the victim's browser parses the HTML page. In this case, the data is sent at in on line . The malicious content sent to the web browser often takes the form of a JavaScript segment, but can also include HTML, Flash, or any other type of code that the browser executes. The variety of attacks based on XSS is almost limitless, but they commonly include transmitting private data such as cookies or other session information to the attacker, redirecting the victim to web content controlled by the attacker, or performing other malicious operations on the user's machine under the guise of the vulnerable site. Example 1: The following JavaScript code segment retrieves a response from a large language model (LLM) and displays it to the user. 
<SCRIPT>
var response = llm.invoke(user_prompt);
...
document.write(response);
</SCRIPT>
DOM-based XSS occurs when an attacker can modify a browser's DOM so that client-side code will be executed in an unintended, and potentially dangerous, manner. The output of an LLM is unpredictable, enabling an attacker utilizing prompt engineering techniques to produce unexpected outputs and bypass developer instructions intended to prevent the LLM from producing dangerous responses. As the example demonstrates, XSS vulnerabilities are caused by code that includes unvalidated responses from an LLM. There are three vectors by which an XSS attack can reach a victim: - Data is read directly from the HTTP request and reflected back in the HTTP response. Reflected XSS exploits occur when an attacker causes a user to supply dangerous content to a vulnerable web application, which is then reflected back to the user and executed by the web browser. The most common mechanism for delivering malicious content is to include it as a parameter in a URL that is posted publicly or emailed directly to victims. URLs constructed in this manner constitute the core of many phishing schemes, whereby an attacker convinces victims to visit a URL that refers to a vulnerable site. After the site reflects the attacker's content back to the user, the content is executed and proceeds to transfer private information, such as cookies that might include session information, from the user's machine to the attacker or perform other nefarious activities. - The application stores dangerous data in a database or other trusted data store. The dangerous data is subsequently read back into the application and included in dynamic content. Persistent XSS exploits occur when an attacker injects dangerous content into a data store that is later read and included in dynamic content. From an attacker's perspective, the optimal place to inject malicious content is in an area that is displayed to either many users or particularly interesting users. Interesting users typically have elevated privileges in the application or interact with sensitive data that is valuable to the attacker. If one of these users executes malicious content, the attacker can perform privileged operations on behalf of the user or gain access to sensitive data belonging to the user. - A source outside the application produces potentially dangrous data, such as an LLM, stores dangerous data in a database, or retrieves data from another data store. This dangerous data is subsequently read back into the application as trusted data and included in dynamic content.
Description.Recommendations:
To prevent XSS, ensure that validation occurs in the required places and that relevant properties are set to prevent vulnerabilities.
Because XSS vulnerabilities occur when an application includes malicious data in its output, one logical approach is to encode data immediately before it leaves the application or is written to the DOM. Responses from an AI model are unpredictable and subject to user manipulation. Therefore, the application cannot implicitly rely on the safety of this or any other data. This means that the best way to prevent AI based XSS vulnerabilities is to validate or encode everything that leaves the application destined for the user.
If input containing special characters must be accepted and displayed accurately, validation must encode any special characters to remove their significance. A complete list of ISO 8859-1 encoded values for special characters is provided as part of the official HTML specification [2].
Many application servers attempt to limit an application's exposure to cross-site scripting vulnerabilities by providing implementations for the functions responsible for setting certain specific HTTP response content that perform validation for the characters essential to a cross-site scripting attack. Do not rely on the server running your application to make it secure. For any developed application, there are no guarantees about which application servers it will run on during its lifetime. As standards and known exploits evolve, there are no guarantees that application servers will continue to stay in sync.
